alignment.note: Greek καί + future ἔσεσθε ('and you will be') is rendered in Syriac as a single prefixed-conjugation verb ܘܬܗܘܘܢ (waw-conjunction fused to the imperfect of h-w-w), whereas Latin separates Et + eritis as in Greek. The Syriac collapses conjunction and copula into one morphological unit.

Greek μισούμενοι is a present passive participle ('being hated') paired with the copula to form a periphrastic future; Syriac ܣܢܝܐܝܢ is a predicative passive participle of s-n-a; Latin uses the dative-of-agent idiom odio (esse) omnibus ('to be an object of hatred to all'), a substantival construction rather than a participle.

Greek marks agency explicitly with ὑπό + genitive and Syriac with the preposition ܡܢ; the Latin expresses agency through the bare dative omnibus without a preposition, a difference of syntactic strategy for the agent of passivity.

Greek πάντων ('all [people]', masc. gen. pl.) and Latin omnibus are plural substantival adjectives, whereas Syriac ܟܠܢܫ is a fixed compound (kol-nāš, 'everyone') functioning as a collective singular — a typical Syriac idiom for universal personal reference.

Greek uses article + noun (τὸ ὄνομά) and Latin the bare noun nomen; the Syriac ܫܡܝ fuses the noun ('name') with the first-person possessive suffix, while Greek and Latin both append a separate possessive pronoun in the following token.

The first-person genitive μου / meum stands as a separate enclitic/pronoun in Greek and Latin, but in Syriac the possession is borne by the pronominal suffix on ܫܡܝ in the preceding group; hence no standalone pronoun token exists here in the Peshitta.

All three attest the adversative connective (Greek δέ, Syriac ܕܝܢ, Latin autem) in second position after a fronted element. Greek and Latin front the substantival article/relative (ὁ / Qui); Syriac fronts the agent-preposition ܡܢ, yielding a slightly different ordering of the same clausal constituents.

Greek substantivises an aorist participle ὁ ὑπομείνας ('the one having endured') and Latin uses a relative clause with future-perfect Qui...sustinuerit; Syriac employs a relative-marked imperfect ܕܢܣܝܒܪ (d- + imperfect of s-b-r), expressing the same future-conditional sense through a finite relative construction.

Greek σωθήσεται and Latin salvus erit denote 'will be saved' (passive of σῴζω / periphrastic salvus + esse), implying deliverance; Syriac ܢܚܐ (imperfect of kh-y-a, 'to live') renders the idea as 'will live/be made alive', a cognate of Hebrew חַי, shifting the nuance from salvation toward life — a characteristic Syriac lexical preference.
